sec.title: Background
sec.p: The aim of the current analyses of a phase 3 randomized controlled trial conducted in Japan was to assess the long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant 75 mg, taken for up to 52 weeks, for the preventive treatment of migraine.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The study included adults in Japan with a history of 4–18 migraine attacks/month of moderate or severe pain intensity. After 12 weeks’ double-blind treatment with rimegepant 75 mg or placebo every other day, participants took open-label rimegepant 75 mg every other day and additionally as needed on nonscheduled dosing days (maximum one dose of rimegepant 75 mg per calendar day), for up to 40 weeks. Safety assessments included adverse events and hepatic function. Effectiveness endpoints included change in monthly migraine days, medication use, and changes in migraine-related quality of life and disability.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 496 participants who received double-blind treatment, 458 participants were treated with rimegepant in the open-label-extension phase (mean age 43.9 years, 90.8% female) for a mean of 37.5 weeks. During the open-label extension phase, the most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis (25.1%) and COVID-19 (13.1%); the rate of adverse events leading to rimegepant discontinuation was 1.3% and the rate of serious adverse events was 0.9%. Aminotransferases >3x the upper limit of normal occurred in four (0.9%) participants during the open-label extension phase; none of these participants had concurrent elevations with total bilirubin >2x upper limit of normal. For the open-label extension phase overall, monthly migraine days of any pain intensity reduced by a mean (95% confidence interval [95% CI]) of –4.5 (95% CI –4.8, –4.2) days with 55.4% (95% CI 50.8, 59.9) of participants experiencing ≥50% reductions compared with the observation period. The use of acute treatments for migraine was low through the open-label extension phase. Improvements from baseline in Migraine-Specific Quality-of-Life Questionnaire v2.1, Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS), and EQ visual analog scale were observed through the 52-week study.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Sustained effectiveness, with a favorable safety profile, was observed in treatment with rimegepant 75 mg taken up to once daily for up to 52 weeks.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The recurring headache, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia associated with migraine [1] have a detrimental effect on all aspects of patients’ lives, including mental health, quality of life and work productivity [2]. Worldwide, migraine is a leading cause of disability [3]. The long-term prognosis is variable, but for many patients migraine requires management over many years [4–6] and both preventive and acute treatment options.

There is a substantial unmet need for the preventive treatment of migraine [7, 8]. Many patients are not prescribed a preventive treatment [9] and traditional treatments (including beta-blockers, antidepressants, antiepileptics, and calcium channel blockers) can have limited efficacy and poor tolerability [10–12] resulting in high discontinuation rates [9, 13]. Injectable calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) monoclonal antibodies are recommended for migraine prophylaxis [10, 11, 14] but their long half lives mean immediate cessation is not possible [15], and patients may prefer oral treatments to injections [16].

Rimegepant is an oral, small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonist that is effective for both the acute treatment of migraine [17–21] and the preventive treatment of migraine [22, 23]. The long-term effectiveness and safety of open-label rimegepant have been demonstrated in studies conducted in the United States [24, 25], but have not yet been reported elsewhere.

A phase 3 study conducted in Japan was the first double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine to be conducted outside of the United States and the second globally [23]. It comprised a 12-week double-blind treatment (DBT) phase, during which participants took rimegepant 75 mg or placebo every other day (EOD), followed by a 40-week open-label extension (OLE) phase, during which participants took rimegepant 75 mg EOD on scheduled dosing days and as needed (PRN) when they had a migraine on nonscheduled dosing days. In the DBT phase, the efficacy of rimegepant was superior to placebo with a favorable safety profile [23], extending the evidence base for preventive treatment beyond the study conducted in the United States [22].

There are currently few long-term data available for rimegepant, and these are exclusively from the USA [24, 25]. The aim of the current analyses of the phase 3 study conducted in Japan [23] was to evaluate long-term safety, as well as effectiveness, in participants in Japan treated with open-label rimegepant for up to 40 weeks, and in those who were randomized to rimegepant during the DBT phase and subsequently took rimegepant in the OLE phase for up to 52 weeks in total.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This prospective, phase 3, double-blind, randomized, multicenter trial (study number C4951021 or BHV3000-309; NCT05399485), conducted at 44 study sites in Japan, evaluated the effectiveness and safety of rimegepant 75 mg orally disintegrating tablet (ODT) compared with placebo for the preventive treatment of migraine. The study comprised a 28-day observation phase (OP), a 12-week DBT phase, and a 40-week OLE phase (Fig. 1). Full methodology and the primary findings for this study were reported previously [23]. The current analyses include both the 12-week randomized DBT phase and the 40-week OLE phase.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: Participants were eligible for the OLE phase of the study if they (1) completed the DBT phase, (2) continued to meet all eligibility criteria for the study, (3) had been compliant with their use of the electronic diary (eDiary), and (4) laboratory results were within acceptable ranges at the end of the DBT phase. Briefly, key eligibility criteria for the study were adults with a ≥ 1 year history of migraine (with or without aura) consistent with a diagnosis according to International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3) [1]; onset of migraine before 50 years of age; migraine attacks lasting, on average, 4–72 h if untreated; 4–18 migraine attacks/month (4 weeks) of moderate or severe pain intensity within the last 3 months prior to the screening visit; four or more migraine days during the OP; ≤18 headache days during the OP; and the ability to distinguish migraine attacks from tension-type or cluster headache. Excluded were brainstem aura (basilar migraine), hemiplegic migraine, or retinal migraine; headache (migraine or non-migraine) occurring ≥ 19 days per month in any of the 3 months prior to screening; and history with current evidence of uncontrolled, unstable, or recently diagnosed cardiovascular disease (such as ischemic heart disease, coronary artery vasospasm, cerebral ischemia) or myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, percutaneous coronary intervention, cardiac surgery, stroke or transient ischemic attack during the 6 months prior to screening.

Participants were allowed to remain on one background preventive migraine medication (other than CGRP antagonists) throughout the study, provided the dose was stable. Acute treatments (standard of care, including aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, baclofen, acetaminophen, antiemetics, and muscle relaxants) were allowed if needed. The use of triptans was prohibited during the OLE phase as participants used rimegepant as needed for acute treatment. Use of triptans in the OLE phase or ergotamine at any point during the study was recorded as a protocol deviation and counted as acute migraine-specific medication use if administered.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: After 12 weeks of DBT with rimegepant 75 mg or placebo EOD, eligible participants continued open-label treatment with rimegepant for up to 40 additional weeks. During the OLE phase, participants took one rimegepant 75 mg EOD, regardless of migraine status (i.e., scheduled dosing days). On nonscheduled dosing days, if participants experienced a migraine they could take one rimegepant 75 mg on that calendar day to treat the migraine. Therefore, during the OLE phase, participants could take a maximum of one rimegepant 75 mg ODT per calendar day for up to 40 weeks.

sec.title: Procedures and assessments
sec.p: Visits were at screening and baseline, then at Weeks 2, 4, 8, and 12 during the DBT phase and at Weeks 14 and 16, then every 4 weeks until Week 52/end of treatment, during the OLE phase. There was a final follow-up safety visit 14 ± 2 days after the Week 52/end of treatment visit.

Participants used an eDiary every day during study to record migraine occurrence, migraine pain features and associated symptoms, and use of acute migraine medication (i.e., triptan, ergotamine, or other). Japanese versions of the Migraine-Specific Quality-of-Life Questionnaire (MSQoL) v2.1 [26, 27], Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) [28, 29], and EQ visual analog scale (EQ-VAS) as part of the EQ-5D-5 L [30–32] were administered by study investigators and recorded in the eDiary at specified study visits (Weeks 12, 24 and 52).

Participants recorded all concomitant medications, including acute and prophylactic standard of care migraine medications (both prescribed and over the counter) taken during the study in a concomitant medication paper diary.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: Safety was assessed throughout the study, including adverse events (AEs), serious AEs, and AEs leading to study drug discontinuation; clinically relevant (i.e., grade 3–4) laboratory test abnormalities, elevations in alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase >3x upper limit of normal (ULN) concurrent with total bilirubin (TBL) >2x ULN; and hepatic-related AEs and hepatic-related AEs leading to study drug discontinuation.

For each study-month (4-week period), effectiveness endpoints included mean change from the OP in the number of monthly migraine days (MMD) of any pain intensity and of moderate or severe pain intensity, percentages of responders (participants with ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions from the OP in MMD), mean number of acute migraine-specific medication (triptan or ergotamine on any day, or rimegepant on a nonscheduled dosing day during the OLE phase) days per month, and mean number of acute migraine medication (acute migraine-specific medication or other medications to treat headache or aura) days per month. A migraine day was a calendar day with a qualified migraine headache, defined as the onset, continuation or recurrence of migraine with or without aura lasting for ≥ 30 min, associated with nausea and/or vomiting, or photophobia and phonophobia, and/or two or more specified pain features (unilateral location, pulsating quality [throbbing], moderate or severe pain intensity, aggravated by or causing avoidance of routine physical activity [e.g., walking or climbing stairs]); or the use of acute migraine-specific medication.
Mean change from baseline in MSQoL v2.1 domain scores, mean change from baseline in MIDAS scores, and mean change from baseline in EQ-VAS score were evaluated at Weeks 12, 24, and 52.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The current report comprises prespecified analyses of prespecified endpoints for a phase 3 clinical trial, the methodology and primary findings for which have been published previously [23].

Safety was assessed in participants taking ≥ 1 dose of rimegepant in the OLE phase (OLE rimegepant safety analysis set) or in the DBT or OLE phase (DBT or OLE rimegepant safety analysis set). AEs were coded using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities v27.1.

Efficacy and effectiveness were assessed in 3 analysis sets. The DBT efficacy analysis set comprised randomized participants taking ≥ 1 dose of DBT study drug. The DBT migraine analysis set comprised randomized participants taking ≥ 1 dose of DBT study drug who had ≥ 14 days of eDiary efficacy data (not necessarily consecutive) in both the OP and ≥ 1 month (4-week interval) in the DBT phase. The OLE rimegepant migraine analysis set comprised randomized participants who took open-label rimegepant regardless of DBT treatment assignment, that is: randomized participants who took ≥ 1 dose of DBT study drug and ≥ 1 dose of rimegepant during the OLE phase, and who had ≥ 14 days of eDiary efficacy data (not necessarily consecutive) in both the OP and ≥ 1 month (4-week interval) in the OLE phase.

Effectiveness endpoints were assessed for each study month (4-week period), including Month (M) 1 (Weeks > 0 to ≤ 4) through M3 (Weeks > 8 to ≤ 12) during the DBT phase and M4 (Weeks > 12 to ≤ 16) through M13 (Weeks > 48 to ≤ 52) during the OLE phase. MMDs for each study month were prorated to 28 days to account for missing eDiary efficacy data. MMDs were also calculated for each overall treatment phase in its entirety (overall DBT or overall OLE) and prorated to 28 days. Responder analyses for the overall OLE phase were according to individuals’ meeting the reduction criteria from the OP in the number of MMDs for the overall OLE.

Effectiveness endpoints during the OLE phase were prespecified as exploratory endpoints; these data were observed and summarized descriptively. For the MMD endpoints in the OLE phase, intercurrent events were handled using the following estimand strategies: study drug discontinuation was addressed with a while-on-treatment strategy; use of nonstudy prophylactic migraine medication and other nonstudy medications for headache or aura were addressed with a treatment policy strategy; and use of nonstudy acute migraine-specific medication was addressed with a composite strategy.
All statistical analyses were performed using SAS statistical software (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) version 9.4.

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki, International Conference on Harmonization guidelines, Good Clinical Practice, and Good Laboratory Practice. All participants provided written informed consent, and these forms and the protocol received Institutional Review Board/Independent Ethics Committee approval prior to initiation of the study. The list of Institutional Review Boards/Independent Ethics Committees for this study was reported previously [23].

sec.title: Participant disposition and demographics
sec.p: The study, including DBT and OLE phases, was conducted from August 9, 2022, to November 7, 2024. During the DBT phase, 496 participants received study drug and were included in the DBT efficacy analysis set (rimegepant n = 247, placebo n = 249) and 484 participants were included in the DBT migraine analysis set (rimegepant n = 240, placebo n = 244). In the OLE phase, 458 participants were treated with rimegepant and were included in the OLE rimegepant safety analysis set, 478 participants were included in the DBT or OLE rimegepant safety analysis set, and 457 participants were included in the OLE rimegepant migraine analysis set. The rate of discontinuations was low: of the 458 participants treated with rimegepant in the OLE phase, 419 (91.5%) completed the OLE phase (Fig. 2).

sec.p: Demographics were similar according to randomization to rimegepant or placebo during the DBT phase (Table 1). Of the participants treated with open-label rimegepant (n = 458), 29.9% had a history of chronic migraine according to ICHD-3 criteria, mean (standard deviation [SD]) age at migraine onset was 20.0 (8.9) years, the mean (SD) duration of untreated migraine attacks, on average, was 26.3 (18.7) hours, and the primary migraine type was without aura (86.9%) or with aura (13.1%).

sec.p: Overall, participants took rimegepant for a mean (SD) of 37.5 (6.3) weeks during the OLE phase (n = 458) (Table 2).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: During OLE treatment with rimegepant (n = 458) and during up to 52 weeks’ rimegepant treatment (n = 478), AEs were mostly mild-moderate; the most frequent AEs were nasopharyngitis and COVID-19 (25.1% and 13.1%, respectively, in the OLE phase) (Table 3). The rate of AEs leading to rimegepant discontinuation was 1.3% in the OLE phase and 2.1% during up to 52 weeks’ rimegepant treatment (Table 3). The rate of serious AEs was 0.9% in the OLE phase: the four serious AEs were coronavirus infection, nodal osteoarthritis, constipation (considered related to study drug), and hepatic function abnormal (considered related to study drug), all of which were recovered/resolved. The rate of serious AEs was 1.3% during up to 52 weeks’ rimegepant treatment: the six serious AEs were coronavirus infection, COVID 19, pancreatitis acute, nodal osteoarthritis, constipation, and hepatic function abnormal. There were no deaths. The rate of hepatic-related AEs was 3.3% in the OLE phase and 3.6% during up to 52 weeks’ rimegepant treatment (Table 3). The rate of hypertension AEs was 1.3% in the OLE phase and 1.7% during up to 52 weeks’ rimegepant treatment (Table 3); one of the hypertension AEs in the OLE phase was considered related to study medication in a participant assigned double-blind placebo before receiving open-label rimegepant.

sec.p: There were no signals of clinically meaningful toxicity grade shifts from baseline for any of the hematology, serum chemistry, and urinalysis parameters in either treatment group during the OLE phase. During the OLE phase, grade 3 to 4 hematology abnormalities were reported in five participants, grade 3 to 4 serum chemistry abnormalities were reported in 16 participants, and grade 3 to 4 urinalysis abnormalities were reported in four participants (Table S1).

sec.title: Effectiveness
sec.p: Reductions in MMD from the OP were sustained through the 52-week study, including MMD of any pain intensity (Fig. 3A, Table S2) and MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity (Fig. 3B, Table S3). During the OP, participants overall reported a mean (SD) of 9.2 (3.1) MMD of any intensity and 6.3 (3.0) MMD of moderate or severe intensity. In M13 (Weeks > 48 to ≤ 52), participants overall reported a mean of 4.4 (95% CI 4.0, 4.8) MMD of any pain intensity (mean reduction from the OP of − 4.7 [95% CI − 5.1, − 4.3], n = 417) and 2.6 (95% CI 2.3, 2.9) MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity (mean reduction from the OP of − 3.7 [95% CI − 4.0, − 3.4], n = 406]). For the OLE phase overall, participants reported a mean of 4.6 (95% CI 4.3, 4.9) MMD of any pain intensity (mean reduction from the OP of − 4.5 [95% CI − 4.8, − 4.2], n = 457) and 2.7 (95% CI 2.5, 2.9) MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity (mean reduction from the OP of − 3.6 [95% CI − 3.9, − 3.4], n = 445). Of note, effectiveness was comparable regardless of DBT assignment from the first month of open-label rimegepant treatment and throughout the entire duration of the OLE phase (Table S2, Table S3).

sec.p: The percentages of participants achieving ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions from the OP in MMD of any pain intensity (Fig. 4A) and MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity (Fig. 4B) were consistent across the study. In M13 (Weeks > 48 to ≤ 52), 60.0% (95% CI 55.2, 64.7), 33.1% (95% CI 28.6, 37.6), and 12.2% (95% CI 9.1, 15.4) of participants overall (n = 417) experienced ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions, respectively, from the OP in MMD of any pain intensity and 67.5% (95% CI 62.9, 72.0), 45.6% (95% CI 40.7, 50.4), and 28.3% (95% CI 23.9, 32.7) of participants (n = 406) experienced ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions, respectively, from the OP in MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity. During the whole OLE phase, 55.4% (95% CI 50.8, 59.9), 19.7% (95% CI 16.0, 23.3), and 0.9% (95% CI 0.0, 1.7) of participants overall (n = 457) experienced ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions from the OP in MMD of any pain intensity and 66.5% (95% CI 62.1, 70.9), 34.2% (95% CI 29.8, 38.6), and 3.8% (95% CI 2.0, 5.6) of participants (n = 445) experienced ≥ 50%, ≥ 75%, and 100% reductions from the OP in MMD of moderate or severe pain intensity.

sec.p: The use of acute migraine-specific medication (Fig. 5A, Table S4) and acute migraine medication (Fig. 5B, Table S4) was consistently low through the OLE phase. During the OP, participants overall (n = 484) used acute migraine-specific medication on a mean (SD) of 6.3 (4.4) days per month and acute migraine medication on 7.8 (3.4) days per month. In M13 (Weeks > 48 to ≤ 52), participants overall (n = 417) used acute migraine-specific medication on a mean of 1.7 (95% CI 1.5, 1.9) days per month and acute migraine medication on 3.7 (95% CI 3.4, 4.0) days per month. During the whole OLE phase, participants overall (n = 457) used acute migraine-specific medication on 1.7 (95% CI 1.5, 1.8) days per month and acute migraine medication on 3.7 (95% CI 3.5, 4.0) days per month.

sec.p: Improvements from baseline were observed across the study for MSQoL Role Function Restrictive, Role Function Preventive, and Emotional Function domain scores (Fig. 6A, Table S5). At baseline, participants overall (n = 495) had median (Q1, Q3) scores of 68.6 (60.0, 80.0) for Role Function Restrictive, 85.0 (80.0, 95.0) for Role Function Preventive, and 80.0 (66.7, 93.3) for Emotional Function domains of the MSQoL. At Week 52, participants overall (n = 415) had median (Q1, Q3) scores of 82.9 (74.3, 91.4) for Role Function Restrictive (improvement from baseline of median 14.3 [Q1, Q3 2.9, 22.9] and mean 13.8 [95% CI 12.2, 15.4]), 95.0 (85.0, 100.0) for Role Function Preventive (improvement from baseline of median 5.0 [Q1, Q3 0.0, 15.0] and mean 7.5 [95% CI 6.2, 8.8]), and 93.3 (80.0, 100.0) for Emotional Function (improvement from baseline of median 6.7 [Q1, Q3 0.0, 20.0] and mean 11.2 [95% CI 9.6, 12.8]) domains of the MSQoL.

At baseline, participants overall (n = 495) had median (Q1, Q3) scores of 9.0 (3.0, 20.0) for MIDAS Total, 4.0 (1.0, 9.0) for Absenteeism, and 5.0 (1.0, 10.0) for Presenteeism. Improvements from baseline were observed across the study for EQ-VAS scores (Fig. 6C, Table S5). At baseline, participants overall (n = 494) had a median (Q1, Q3) EQ-VAS score of 80.0 (70.0, 90.0), and at Week 52 (n = 414) had improved to 87.0 (78.0, 91.0): an improvement from baseline of median 1.0 (Q1, Q3 − 5.0, 11.0) and mean 3.7 (95% CI 1.9, 5.6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this was the first trial reporting the long-term safety and effectiveness of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine conducted outside the United States. Sustained effectiveness, with a favorable safety profile, was observed in the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan. The data for the OLE phase were consistent with the DBT phase [23], the previous study of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine conducted in the United States [22], and longer-term open-label data [24, 25, 33]. The dosing regimen for the OLE phase (EOD plus PRN on nonscheduled dosing days) is consistent with the expected clinical use for rimegepant (up to one 75 mg-tablet per calendar day).

As reported previously, the study met its primary efficacy endpoint, with a statistically significant reduction in mean MMD in the last 4 weeks of the DBT phase for rimegepant compared with placebo [23]. The efficacy of rimegepant early in the first month and sustained through the 3-month DBT phase [23] supports the previous findings from the US study [22]. In the current analyses (Fig. 3) there was a considerable decrease in mean MMD from the OP during the entire OLE phase in the overall population. An additional decrease was also observed from the end of the DBT phase (M3) to the start of the OLE phase (M4) in the group treated with rimegepant through both phases. These observations may be the result of assessment bias related to open-label treatment (participants being aware they were receiving active treatment) or may reflect the more real-world setting of the OLE phase. A reduction of similar magnitude was seen in the US study [25].

During the OLE phase, when all participants received rimegepant, the reduction in mean MMD was sustained along with the improvements in most other effectiveness endpoints. In particular, the percentage of participants achieving ≥ 50% reduction in MMD was consistently high through the 52-week study (Fig. 4). These findings of durable effectiveness are in accordance with what was observed in the OLE phase of the US study [25] and are reassuring for the longer-term management of migraine for clinicians and patients alike. A reduction in MMD is a clinically important goal of preventive treatment [34–36] that is associated with better health-related outcomes for patients [37, 38]. In the current study, sustained improvements in patient-reported outcomes (MIDAS, MSQoL, and EQ-VAS) were seen, underlining the long term effectiveness of rimegepant, and its benefits in terms of improvements in headache-related disability, quality of life and health. Although the discontinuation rate was relatively low in this study, with 91.5% of participants completing the OLE phase, it should be noted that the analysis of effectiveness for the OLE adopted a “while on treatment” estimand strategy, whereby only observed data from participants who remained on treatment were included, and no imputation was performed for missing data following treatment discontinuation.

Rimegepant is the only medication that is effective for both the acute [17–21] and preventive [22, 23] treatment of migraine, and therefore offers a comprehensive approach to long-term management. Japanese treatment guidelines recommend the traditional, oral preventive treatments for patients with more than two migraine attacks per month or a history of headache interfering with daily activities on more than three days a month, as well as for patients for whom acute treatments have not worked or are not suitable [14]. Elsewhere, migraine-specific and CGRP-targeted therapies are widely recommended first-line for migraine prophylaxis [35, 39]. Although the injectable CGRP monoclonal antibodies are available in Japan [14], the oral gepants are not yet available.

Rimegepant had a favorable safety profile in the current OLE phase and was well tolerated. As seen in other studies [24, 25, 33], AEs were mostly mild to moderate, most commonly upper respiratory tract infection-related, and rates of hepatic AEs, AEs leading to discontinuation and serious AEs were low. Clinical laboratory tests were mostly unremarkable, and no participants had aminotransferases >3x ULN concurrent with elevations in TBL >2x ULN, replicating the lack of drug-induced liver injury as was confirmed in previous long-term studies with rimegepant [22, 24, 25, 33].

The strengths of this study include its prospective nature and considerable duration (up to 12 months), the large number of participants entering the OLE phase and the low discontinuation rate. Further, the study evaluated numerous important effectiveness and safety endpoints of migraine prevention. The limitations of the OLE phase include the inherent bias of open-label designs and the lack of a comparator arm, which can overestimate treatment effectiveness; because both participants and investigators knew the active treatment was being administered, it is difficult to distinguish the true pharmacological effect of rimegepant from the placebo effect, patient expectation bias, and the natural variations in migraine frequency. Patients with unstable cardiovascular disease and higher frequency of headache were excluded from the study which may somewhat limit the generalizability of the results and requires further studies specific to these patient populations. Triptans were allowed in the DBT phase, but not in the OLE phase, which could affect the generalizability of the results. Efficacy and safety of rimegepant were observed in the DBT phase of this and previous studies under concomitant triptan use [22, 23]. Additionally, no clinically meaningful hemodynamic or pharmacokinetic interactions were observed when rimegepant and triptan were co-administered in healthy adults [40]. The current data are specific to this population from Japan; they are consistent with the results of clinical trials conducted in Japan [21, 23], the USA and China [17–20, 22], and race/ethnicity have no clinically relevant effect on the pharmacokinetics of rimegepant [41].

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Sustained effectiveness and a favorable safety profile were observed in the treatment of migraine in Japan with rimegepant 75 mg taken up to once daily for up to 52 weeks. Together with the primary results from the DBT phase of this study, this evidence from the OLE phase supports and broadens the previous findings of rimegepant for the preventive and long-term treatment of migraine to a wider population.
